one_liner: Constant-time pairing-curve cryptography in Nim whose macro-generated x86-64 MULX/ADCX/ADOX inline assembly beats its own compiler-built field arithmetic.
what_it_does: Constantine is a constant-time elliptic-curve and pairing library aimed at blockchain and zero-knowledge workloads. It covers field, extension-field and curve arithmetic on BN254, BLS12-381 and the Pasta curves, plus MSM, Ethereum BLS signatures, EIP-4844 KZG and the EVM BN254/BLS12-381 precompiles. It is consumed from Nim, or as a C static/shared library built with nimble make_lib, through Rust crates (constantine-sys, constantine-ethereum-kzg, a Halo2 ZAL crate) or Go bindings. The assembly is not a separate API: it is the default build path, and CTT_ASM=0 swaps in the generic compiler path behind the same functions.
how_it_is_fast: Nim macros act as a compile-time assembler. They emit size-specialised inline asm for each limb count: CIOS Montgomery multiplication, squaring and reduction ('sparebit' variants for moduli with a free top bit). On x86-64 these use MULX with the two independent carry chains of ADCX/ADOX, which C compilers do not emit. A runtime hasAdx() check picks the ADX kernels for 2-6 limbs and otherwise falls back to plain ADD/ADC assembly. The assembly also sidesteps GCC's poor _addcarry_u64 code generation (setc/addb round trips, shown in README-PERFORMANCE.md), and the inline-asm blocks keep the compiler from turning branchless constant-time code back into branches. ARM64 has its own inline-asm generators (2-8 limbs).
when_to_use: Ethereum consensus or execution clients and provers that need constant-time BLS12-381 or BN254 primitives (BLS signatures, KZG for EIP-4844, EIP-2537 and BN254 precompiles) on x86-64 servers with ADX and BMI2 (Broadwell or Zen and later).
Builds that must use GCC: the asm path removes most of GCC's carry-handling penalty, and the first-party figure is 2.4x for GCC with inline asm over plain GCC.
Rust, Go or C projects that want a pairing-curve backend with no runtime dependencies (GMP is only used in tests).
Many-core MSM and batched KZG verification, where its threadpool runs nested parallel loops (three parallel MSMs, each with three nested parallel loops, for batch KZG verification).
when_not_to_use: When you need an audited or stable library. The README carries an 'experimental' badge and says the library is provided as-is, without guarantees, at least until it is audited and formal proofs exist.
When you need evidence that the assembly pays off on your platform. No asm-off numbers or external-library comparisons are published; the charts are asm-on Constantine timings only.
CPUs or VMs without ADX. The fallback x86 asm is marked in limbs_montgomery.nim as 'faster than GCC but slower than Clang', so a Clang build there may do better with CTT_ASM=0.

MSVC (not configured; Windows is tested with MinGW only), Apple Clang with LTO (no Intel asm syntax), GCC 15 with LTO (#588: cyclotomic exponentiation tests fail, which affects BLS signatures and KZG), or GCC on ARM64 (#582: 'more than 30 operands in asm').
Fields wider than 6 limbs (384 bits) on x86-64, and full-width moduli with no spare bit: Montgomery multiplication there takes the compiler path (mulMont_FIPS or generic CIOS), not the ADX kernels.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime; build needs Nim v2.2.0 plus a C compiler (Clang recommended); Rust crates by git dependency invoke nimble with CC=clang from build.rs; Go bindings link the static library
integration.min_toolchain: Nim v2.2.0; GCC 7+ or Clang 14+ (Clang 14 for -masm=intel, required with LTO); Homebrew Clang on macOS
integration.platforms: x86-64 (MULX/ADCX/ADOX kernels with runtime ADX dispatch, ADD/ADC asm fallback), x86-32 asm, ARM64 inline asm with Clang (GCC broken per #582), generic code elsewhere; Linux, macOS, Windows via MinGW
integration.thread_safety: not documented for the primitives; the core arithmetic does no heap allocation, CPU-feature globals are set at load, and parallel MSM/KZG APIs take an explicit threadpool

gotchas: The asm-versus-compiler comparison is not like-for-like. The release flags set no -march, -mbmi2 or -madx, so the CTT_ASM=0 build cannot use MULX at all; only the ADCX/ADOX dual carry chain is something compilers truly cannot emit. In addition, bench_fields_template.nim's Multiplication and Squaring loops reuse loop-invariant inputs with preventOptimAway placed only before the loop. The asm kernels are 'asm volatile' with a 'memory' clobber and cannot be hoisted, while the plain C path can be, and bench_blueprint.nim itself warns that 'the simplest operations might be optimized away by the compiler'.

The 'CPU cycles' column in the published benchmarks (for example Fp[BLS12_381] multiplication 68 cycles) is rdtsc ticks at the nominal clock; the harness prints a warning that turbo and overclocking skew it.

Every generated asm block that writes through a pointer carries a full 'memory' clobber (a comment says the Poly1305 MAC test fails without it). This forces the compiler to reload operands around each kernel and limits scheduling across calls. Issue #446 (open) reports that a 1.7x field-arithmetic advantage on secp256k1 shrinks to a 0.85x disadvantage at the elliptic-curve level, traced to cache misses.

The README is stale on ARM: it says 'Assembly is planned for ARM', and the Rust install notes say Constantine has no ARM assembly, yet constantine/math/arithmetic/assembly holds limbs_asm_*_arm64.nim generators that config.nim enables (UseASM_ARM64) for any GCC-compatible compiler.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Constantine over CryptOpt when you need a complete constant-time pairing-curve stack (BLS signatures, KZG, EVM precompiles, MSM) with asm specialised per limb count. Pick CryptOpt, or CRYPTOGAMS-style perlasm kernels, when you need field arithmetic for Curve25519, P-256 or secp256k1 checked for equivalence against Fiat Cryptography with measured gains over GCC and Clang, which Constantine does not offer (its README says formal proofs are not yet produced).
verified_claims_summary: First-party prose only, in README-PERFORMANCE.md: MULX/ADCX/ADOX assembly is 'up 60%' faster for BLS12-381 (6-limb) field arithmetic and '~60% faster than Clang', and there is a '2.4x perf ratio' between plain GCC and GCC with inline asm. No CPU, compiler version, table or run log stands behind these figures, and the same file's GCC-versus-Clang figures disagree (up to 2x, ~50%, 20-25%). The published charts (Ryzen 7 7840U; i9-9980XE for BN254 MSM) show asm-on Constantine timings only. The nimble bench tasks can reproduce an on/off pair (outputs are suffixed _asmIfAvailable or _noAsm via CTT_ASM=0), subject to the harness caveats above.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-04, Nim 2.2.x regression #628 open), MIT OR Apache-2.0 and copyable. It is unaudited and labelled experimental, its speedup over its own compiler path is an undocumented first-party claim, and toolchain-specific failures (GCC 15 LTO #588, GCC ARM64 asm #582) mean Clang is the only well-trodden build.
